utterances.speaker: JUDGE CANIVELL
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the Presiding Judge, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honour. This is case number IT-95-11-PT, the Prosecutor versus Milan Martic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CANIVELL
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CANIVELL
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Madam Registrar. May we have the appearances, please, for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honour. For the Prosecution, my name is Hildegard Uertz-Retzlaff, and I appear with my colleague Nisha Valabhji, and we are accompanied by case manager, Lakshmie Walpita.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CANIVELL
utterances.text: Thank you. And for the Defence, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honour. I am the lead counsel for Milan Martic, Predrag Milovancevic, and this is my legal assistant.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: And the interpreter did not get the name, unfortunately.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CANIVELL
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Martic, please, can you hear the proceedings in a language that you can understand?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CANIVELL
utterances.text: Thank you. You may sit down. With this Status Conference doesn't have much matters to deal with, fortunately, as I understand. First of all, I will speak about the pending motions, and I am going to read the proposed decision about them. First, the Defence motion for provisional release. The Chamber will take a decision as soon as it is informed of the commencement for the possible date of the commencement of the trial. No, that's not in reference with that -- but I mean, as soon as possible we'll take a reference -- a decision about that. The Defence motion for recommendation has validly done the filings concerning the Defence objections on the admission of the Prosecution expert and witness' statements. The parties were informed during the meeting held pursuant to Rule 65 ter yesterday, Wednesday, 18 May, 2005, that the Chamber would render an oral decision on this issue, chiefly the Defence motion for recognizing as validly done the Defence's submissions concerning objections to the admission of expert and witness' statements or testimonies. The Chamber also takes note of the filings made by the parties in relation to the Defence motion to recognise as validly done the filings concerning the admission of written evidence requested by the Prosecution. The Chamber finds that good cause exists in the present case in accordance with Rule 127 of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence. In particular, the Chamber considers that it is in the interests of justice, in particular for the expeditiousness of the proceedings, to consider as validly done the findings made in relation to the Defence objections to the admission of written statements. I would like to add also that the Chamber will deal with the Defence objections, despite the fact that some of them had been filed out of time. Nevertheless, I have to and I would like to remind the Defence of its obligation to respect the lines which are enshrined within the Tribunal's Rules of Procedure and Evidence. As they have been told before, I insist that no further filings out of time will be accepted, unless there are very good grounds for such late filings. I have been informed also about the situation on the agreed facts. I know that the Defence is still not decided or there's not agreement in accepting some of these facts that are put forward as agreed facts. I refer to the last two ones of the 45 that are included. And, I know that a new 65 ter meeting is being, tentatively at least, scheduled for next month on the 23rd, I believe, to deal with this matter as well as with other matters that couldn't be decided, not yesterday, not today. I would like to add the Chamber wishes to be briefed about the outcome of these proceedings. And now I could refer to Mr. Martic's situation, about primarily his mental and physical condition. Tell me, Mr. Martic, do you feel in good condition physically and mentally?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if I may, I would like to speak after the Prosecution and the Defence taking the floor, if you agree. I would prefer to first listen to what they have to say and then make a comment of my own.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CANIVELL
utterances.text: After the Prosecution? But I haven't asked the Prosecution about that. It's for you to answer if you are feeling well mentally and physically to keep waiting for the hearing of your case. Do you have any problems with your health?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank God, I'm okay, but I would like to say a few things in relation to my case having had the opportunity to listen to what the Prosecution and the Defence say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CANIVELL
utterances.text: I'm not so sure the Prosecution -- has the Prosecution anything to comment on or to say about Mr. Martic's health?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. But actually as we had the -- the meeting yesterday, which was quite extensive, I don't actually have anything to say, except for perhaps there is room for some more agreement on facts, and I think before the 65 ter conference, the next one, we -- the Defence and the Prosecution will meet and discuss it. So we may come up with a proposal already so that the 65 ter conference, the next one, can be brief. That's actually all I can say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CANIVELL
utterances.text: Well, thank you. That is a very good idea, because what is necessary is that you relate, the parties, between yourselves so as to try to make going as expeditiously as possible this case. But I believe that Mr. Milovancevic wants also to say something. Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. Thank you. I would just like to tell the Trial Chamber that I am fully aware of the fact that we must file our documents in good time. As you've mentioned, we have two submissions that we would like to be accepted as if it had been done on time. Let me just point out that we did initially file them within deadlines, but the secretariat, for the reasons we don't know, were delayed by more than a month. And as soon as we got the requests, we replied as soon as possible, and it is for this reason that we have submitted the request for them to be admitted as if they had been on time. I just thought I should explain this in order to avoid you having the wrong impression of us not obeying the Rules. And just one other brief point, but an important one, the pre- trial brief was submitted last year. We know that there is more than 14.000 pages there, and all that will be revealed in the course of the trial as proof. And then meanwhile, we'll be working with witnesses, et cetera, and meanwhile we got about thousands of pages from the Prosecution. And considering the situation, I am obliged to tell the Trial Chamber that the Defence has been put in a position which is not at all equal to that of the Prosecution, in the sense that we have no funds for -- we haven't had anything for 14 months, and this interferes with the rights of the accused. Our investigators have not been working for the past 14 months because of that. And now this is the fourth Status Conference on the occasion of which we must appeal to you to have some understanding for the accused's situation. I mean, the funds we did have were put to good use in the best possible way, but now, if we compare our situation to that of the Prosecution - I mean, and it is not our position that we have to worry about but the position of the accused - and I think this is an important piece of information for the Trial Chamber. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CANIVELL
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. I am going to answer you before the second point, and we will speak about the first later on. It's nothing that it can be done by this Pre-Trial Judge about defending that you insist. In most occasions we are meeting about lacking. So I couldn't give you an answer about that. But I am not only confident but sure that you will be able, with the help of Mr. Sekulic, I am sure that both of you will be able to overcome whatever difficulties you will have to keep going on in correction with this case. So would you excuse me for a moment. Ms. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CANIVELL
utterances.text: Well, as for the problems that you seem to have experienced with the time limits for your filings, I know yesterday you were given explanations about one of these cases. They went as far as the registrar knew what had happened. And of course, if you remember well, and I am well informed, the same person of the registry, Madam Kelly Philpott, present here, told you that if you ever had any doubts about any case she would be very happy to help you find out what had been the case. So I suppose that with that the problem is settled in correction with you, with respect from the Tribunal. Well, it's another -- yes, a moment. It's another question which I would like to ask you. You had problems, Mr. Martic, or you don't have any in communicating with your counsel in the preparation of your defence?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, this is the fifth or the sixth time you've asked me this question, and I've always told you that I'm more than happy with my Defence team. What I would like to say, in order to support my lawyers, in pointing out that the secretariat has not been working properly, because my rights have been interfered with. More than a year -- for more than a year people have been working without adequate resources, that interferes with my rights and the rights of my defence. And I mean furthermore, the secretariat keeps trying to make our lives difficult on a daily basis basically. But I'm not going to go into any details here because I won't go into this at this point. It would be inappropriate. But I would really like to know when is the trial finally going to start, because I've been here for about four years. I wonder whether I'm going to go down in the Guinness Book of Records for my length of detention before trial. And I mean, what is the point of the length of this detention without the trial date even having been set? Is it some kind of psychological pressure being brought to bear in order for me to somehow reach some -- some kind of agreement and admit to something that I have not committed? If that's the whole point, I will have to disappoint you and tell you no matter how long you keep me here you won't succeed, because my people say that it is very important to keep face. And that means that I've decided to defend myself on the basis of the truth and argument, and I feel I am 100 per cent innocent, and I do hope that on the basis of arguments, put forward with the help of my Defence team, I shall be able to prove this. And it is for this reason that it is unclear to me for what reason I am being held here before the trial can commence. And this is something that I've asked many times. And as to the provisional release, I said this to you three years ago: Don't release me provisionally, put me on trial. I'm not afraid of this trial. I don't know what your arguments are. Why do I have to wait for five years? Apparently, I am going to have to wait for five years. And since I am presumed innocent from your point of view, I am still innocent for as long as you don't prove me guilty in the course of that trial. And so innocent as I am, who knows for how long I'm going to rot here. And well, that's what I want to know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CANIVELL
utterances.text: Thank you for your words. I understand very well -- please sit down. I understand very well your impatience about your case being heard by this Court. I am afraid that it's not still possible to start, and you know very well - perhaps that's been told to you - that we don't have enough courtrooms to be working. You know that we are working morning and afternoons so as not to lose a single moment. And we have also the problem with the number of Judges, you know. So be sure that we are trying to enter your case in the docket as soon as possible, and it's already thought that perhaps in the next -- after the summer we would be beginning the case. And I am very sorry. It's the most I can tell you about. And I understand very well your situation. Well, I believe that Mr. Milovancevic wanted to also express himself. Please go ahead, Mr. Milovancevic. You had something to say? Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, just a brief explanation. I do understand that the Appeal Chamber has already decided this, and I haven't asked you to make another decision now because I know it's impossible. As to the Defence position, I would simply like to tell you that in July last year we put a request to the Registrar for additional resources. That request was turned down in February this year, after nine months, as long as nine months, a huge delay if we consider the situation of the accused. He's in detention. And now we are appealing this. We want this decision to be re-examined. And this was the reason why I felt that it would be pertinent for me to point out to you how difficult the Defence team's situation is at the moment. We are really not in an equal position with regard to the Prosecution. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CANIVELL
utterances.text: I understand what are your concerns, but it's nothing more I can tell you about funding for your case, I mean, the case you are defending. You have got already the decision from the Appeals Chamber. And whatever circumstances that may follow after that, you have to see with the Registrar what is possible to be done. So I'm sorry, I cannot give you any other help on the matter for the time being. I wonder, is there any other subject that you would like to suggest? No?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, I just want to correct something, because Mr. Martic said he's sitting here for four years. That's not true. He's here for three years. I think it should not be exaggerated. It's a long time, that's for sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CANIVELL
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: That's for sure. But it shouldn't be said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CANIVELL
utterances.text: I appreciate very much your explaining that, but it's completely understandable. From the bar I had already noticed that, but I couldn't object to Mr. Martic. Because when you are in the position he is, years may be more standard than they really are. So you would like to explain something else? Go ahead, Mr. Martic, please. Yes. Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, obviously either the translation was wrong or madam has misunderstood. I don't want to give the impression that I'm somehow not all right. I have started my fourth year here, and that's true. On the 15th of May, it has been a full three years, which means that I've just started my fourth year here, so that's what I meant. Either you misunderstood or the interpreter was not good enough. I'm still not sick in the head, you know, just in case you were wondering.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CANIVELL
utterances.text: It's okay. Don't worry, Mr. Martic. None of us has thought any ill-faith on your side about that, but we understand what is the situation and it's clear what is said by both sides, both parties. Well, if anything else is not to be brought about in this case, I will end this meeting. Of course, as is provided for in the Rules, we'll have to meet again in no more than four months, 120 more days, for another Status Conference, which means around the end of September. Let's hope that at this moment the case may have probably - I don't know - surely started. So I conclude this meeting, and not without expressing to both parties and to the personnel that has helped with the carrying-out of this ceremony, and thus we adjourn. Thank you.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the Status Conference adjourned at
